Guitar / Daily routine

Ten minutes, one musical idea.

Keep A minor as your reference and connect notes, pentatonic phrases, triads and rhythm.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Understand

Use the four beats below. Numbers are beats; & marks the halfway point. A down arrow means downstroke, an up arrow means upstroke, and a dash is a silent motion.

Standard tuning: E A D G B E, from the thickest string to the thinnest.

Make the connection

Use ten minutes as a starting format, not a deadline for progress. Tune first. Pick one measurable task, such as four clean chord changes or two bars without losing time. Keep a short note of tempo and the place that failed; this makes the next session specific.

Play it

2 min: find A. 2 min: play A C D E G. 2 min: connect two A minor triads. 2 min: repeat the rhythm slowly. 2 min: make a short phrase and play it without the screen.

The first bar alternates a one-beat sound and a one-beat rest. The second replaces the first beat with two half-beat attacks. Keep beats 2 and 4 silent. Guitar and ukulele use A minor; bass uses A. Listen to how a small rhythmic change alters the phrase.

Six lines, from top to bottom: e B G D A E. String 1 is the thin E. The examples use standard tuning without a capo. Move the hand when needed instead of forcing a wide stretch.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

Read the example as text
  1. Bar 1
    1. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A + String 2 (B), Fret 1, C + String 1 (e), Fret 0, E · 1 beats
    2. Rest · 1 beats
    3. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A + String 2 (B), Fret 1, C + String 1 (e), Fret 0, E · 1 beats
    4. Rest · 1 beats
  2. Bar 2
    1. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A + String 2 (B), Fret 1, C + String 1 (e), Fret 0, E · ½ beats
    2. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A + String 2 (B), Fret 1, C + String 1 (e), Fret 0, E · ½ beats
    3. Rest · 1 beats
    4. String 3 (G), Fret 2, A + String 2 (B), Fret 1, C + String 1 (e), Fret 0, E · 1 beats
    5. Rest · 1 beats

A mistake to avoid

Repeating the whole exercise at speed can repeat the same mistake. Isolate the transition that failed, practise it slowly, then reconnect the bars. Stop and reset if your hand becomes tense.

Listen and check

Count out loud. If the change of chord interrupts your pulse, stay on one chord and slow down. Add the change only when the motion is steady.

Ready for the next step?

Make three clean repetitions before increasing the tempo a little. Finish by recording the two bars once and checking whether both the notes and the silences stay in time.

Choose a lesson

Fretboard notes ↗

A fret is one semitone. The same note appears in several places: use the open strings and the 12th fret as landmarks.

Pentatonic ↗

A minor pentatonic uses A C D E G. Learn a small area first, then turn it into a phrase.

Triads ↗

A triad contains a root, a third and a fifth. The three shapes below contain the same A minor notes: A C E.

Chords ↗

Choose a root to see all its chords. Compare open, barre and compact shapes, then use a position that suits the song and your hand.

Reading tablature ↗

Lines tell you the strings, numbers tell you the frets, and rhythm tells you when. Read two short examples, then decode the common technique symbols.
